source.title: Extraction of espresso coffee by using gradient of temperature. Effect on physicochemical and sensorial characteristics of espresso
source.original_full_text_access: Original nine-page article transcription on coauthor-linked Academia.edu listing, inspected Methods section 2, Tables 2-4, Sensory 2.6, Results 3.1-3.4, Conclusions 4; journal title/DOI verified independently on University of Girona and PubMed.
source.confidence: Study identity and designs independently corroborated; typed HTML may have extraction or table-column artifacts; paper raw data and replicates not reanalyzed.

evidence_checks.claim: Experimental conditions compare 88 to 93 C ramp-up, 90 C flat, 93 to 88 C ramp-down across Robusta, natural Arabica and washed Arabica using an XCelsius Rancilio espresso system near 9 atm; two espressos were prepared per extraction with 15 +/- 0.5 g coffee and approximately 25 +/- 2.5 mL beverage over 25 +/- 5 s.
evidence_checks.strength: controlled experimental conditions in original primary text; not general espresso design
evidence_checks.uncertainty: grind varies and sample counting needs original raw data

evidence_checks.claim: Researchers adjusted grind for each coffee and temperature to attain output volume/time, so gradients were not an isolated single-control intervention. Tables report coffee-dependent physicochemical differences (foam, caffeine, pH, solids, polyphenols) and no universal monotonic response.
evidence_checks.strength: direct full-text methods plus three numeric tables; observational comparisons within controlled setup
evidence_checks.uncertainty: unable to independently hash/read PDF plots; treatment-varying grind confounds attribution

evidence_checks.claim: Trained eleven-person panel rated ten traditional espresso attributes on 0-10 scores, not DIC's personal five-taste outcome and not a within-person next-shot response. The study favored ramp-up in its own evaluated coffee set, but also notes chemistry-to-perceived taste relationship is complex and not one-to-one.
evidence_checks.strength: original human panel descriptive evidence, limited external validity
evidence_checks.uncertainty: no randomized same-user next-shot DIC experiment, no consumer five-rating validation

evidence_checks.claim: The Methods section uses p<0.05 for initial ANOVA, followed by Tukey HSD multiple comparisons at significance level 10% (p<0.1). Statistical letter annotations in Tables 2-4 should not be advertised as uniform 5% confirmatory evidence.
evidence_checks.uncertainty: no reanalysis of sample distributions or multiplicity, extraction formatting uncertain

live_source_crosswalk.behavior: Current configurable optional measured temperature is a scalar in shot and recommendation, with an existing condition-limited 1 C cooler suggestion for astringency and no programmable per-shot temperature ramp. The paper compares actual dynamic temperature trajectories; it cannot validate a scalar-temperature correction or establish advice efficacy.
live_source_crosswalk.locked_boundary: Keep existing five tastes, original temperature and other measurements, machine capability controls, one-change advice, private history, and current Locked numeric targets. Do not infer authorization to collect new profile data or add presets.

proposal.gap: No current evidence that adding ramp programming to DIC is a useful, controllable or consented recommendation feature across members; physical equipment support varies.
options: A: preserve existing optional single-temperature feature and avoid claiming paper-based effectiveness (preferred now).
B: separately seek owner-scoped equipment-capability and research-evaluation proposal with exact logging/consent/privacy safeguards; no coding absent approval.
proposal.impact: No numerical or taste/quality claims; no release item or app changes.
